MHHS2402 · Week 4 · A/Prof Mark Butlin

Respiratory regulation — the inputs that set your breathing

How the body decides how much to breathe: the feedback loop that keeps blood O2, CO2 and pH in range, the sensors that read them, the reflexes that override them, and the brainstem centre that turns it all into rate & depth. Built from your lecture, using its own figures.

Covers 5 learning objectives Figures 8 plates from your lecture Recall 6 section checklists

§0Orientation · LO1

Homeostasis & the feedback loop

Breathing is a controlled variable — so first, what a control system actually needs.

The whole lecture answers one question: what makes you breathe more or less? Before the sensors and centres, you need the shape of the answer. Every regulated variable in the body — temperature, glucose, blood gases — sits inside the same four-part loop. Get the loop, and every later detail slots into it.

Homeostasis is dynamic balance, not rest

Homeostasis is the process of holding a variable (temperature, pH, blood flow, blood gases) near an optimal level. The key word is dynamic: it is about balance, not about being "at rest". Staying in range often demands constant change — think of maintaining blood pH during exercise, blood glucose after eating, or body temperature on a hot day. The system is always working to stay still.

A control loop needs four things

  1. Change (stimulus) — something in the body or environment must actually change.
  2. Detect (sensor) — something must be able to sense that change.
  3. Process (centre) — something must interpret the detector's signal and decide.
  4. Action (effector) — the decision is sent to the respiratory muscles to change minute ventilation.
Label Key — following the loop clockwise
Stimulus
The change that starts everything — e.g. a fall in blood oxygen. No change, no response.
Sensor
The detector (here a peripheral chemosensor; a thermostat's is a thermometer). It converts a physical/chemical change into a signal.
Input signal
The afferent line carrying the reading to the brain — an electrical impulse along the glossopharyngeal nerve.
Processing centre
The respiratory centre (the thermostat's circuit): it weighs the input and decides the response.
Output signal
The efferent command — motor impulses to the somatic motor neurons driving the breathing muscles.
Effect
The effector's action: a change in ventilation (the heater turning on/off).
Response
The loop closing — an opposing change in blood oxygen that cancels the original stimulus.

Trace Plate 0.1 once and you have the skeleton of the entire lecture: §2 fills in the sensors, §4 fills in the processing centre and its outputs, and §1 defines the variables being sensed.

Reasoning · why the "you don't think it" framing matters

Respiratory rate and tidal volume do not change because you decide they should. If you believe your breathing changed, the exam-safe move is to walk the loop backwards: what physical or chemical thing changed first? how was it detected? where was that signal processed? where was the command sent? Feelings are not inputs — a measurable change in the body or environment is. This is why the rest of the lecture is a catalogue of real detectors, not a discussion of willpower.

§0.1Negative vs positive feedback

Negative feedback opposes the initial change: a variable rises → it is detected and processed → a signal is fed back that lowers it (and vice-versa). Applied to breathing: minute ventilation rises → detected → a signal feeds back that decreases it, and if it falls, a signal increases it. The result is stability around a set point.

Positive feedback amplifies the initial change: a variable rises → detected → a signal is fed back that raises it further. The lecture's example is a social-media post going viral — each re-post makes it more visible, driving still more re-posts. Positive feedback runs away from the set point, so it is rare (and usually dangerous) in ventilation.

Reasoning · why breathing runs on negative feedback

Stability needs a force that pushes back. Negative feedback is self-correcting: every deviation generates its own opposite, so the variable is dragged back toward optimum. Positive feedback is self-reinforcing — useful for committed, all-or-nothing events (childbirth, blood clotting, an action potential's upstroke) but catastrophic for a variable you need held steady. You would not want a small rise in CO2 to trigger changes that raise CO2 further.

Memory hook · the sign tells the story

Negative = "NO, go back" (opposes & stabilises). Positive = "YES, more!" (amplifies & runs away).

R Recall checklist — the loop
  • Homeostasis — dynamic balance around an optimum, not rest.
  • Four parts — change → detect → process → action.
  • No change, no response — breathing follows detected signals, not thoughts.
  • Negative feedback — opposes the change; stabilises minute ventilation.
  • Positive feedback — amplifies the change; rare in ventilation.
§1Blood parameters · LO2

Arterial blood parameters

The three numbers the whole system is defending: O2, CO2 and pH.

If breathing is regulated by negative feedback, we need to name the variables being held steady. There are three: oxygen, carbon dioxide, and pH — and pH is really a read-out of CO2. This section defines their normal values so that "abnormal" (and therefore "correctable") has meaning.

Why gases in blood — in a respiratory lecture?

Because gas exchange is entirely passive: a gas moves from an area of higher partial pressure to one of lower partial pressure, and never the other way. Ventilation exists to keep those partial-pressure gradients pointing the right way at every handover — atmosphere → alveoli → blood → tissue. Plate 1.1 shows the three exchange steps that the numbers must protect.

Label Key — following one O2 molecule down the gradient
Exchange I
Atmosphere → lung (ventilation). Fresh air brings O2 to the alveoli and carries CO2 out — the step breathing directly controls.
Airways / alveoli
The gas-exchange surface: air on one side, capillary blood on the other, a whisper apart.
Exchange II
Lung → blood. O2 diffuses into pulmonary capillary blood; CO2 diffuses out — each down its own partial-pressure gradient.
Pulmonary vs systemic circulation
The transport loop: red = O2-rich, blue = O2-poor. Note the colours swap between the two circulations.
Exchange III
Blood → cells. O2 leaves blood for tissue; CO2 (the waste of cellular respiration) enters blood to be carried back.
Cellular respiration → ATP
The reason for all of it: cells burn O2 and nutrients to make ATP, producing CO2 that must be cleared.
Partial pressures & pH across the compartments (mmHg)
CompartmentPO2PCO2pH
Alveoli~100~40—
Arterial blood85–10035–457.38–7.42
Tissue cells10–30~507.34
Venous blood~40~46~7.37

Read the table as gradients, not trivia: O2 falls (100 → 40) and CO2 rises (40 → 46) exactly where each needs to diffuse. Notice pH dips wherever CO2 is highest — the clue to §1's central idea.

§1.1How the gases are carried

Carbon dioxide travels three ways. Most importantly it dissolves and reacts with water, catalysed by carbonic anhydrase:

CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−

i.e. carbon dioxide + water ⇌ carbonic acid ⇌ hydrogen ions + bicarbonate ions. It is also carried bound to haemoglobin as carbaminohaemoglobin (CO2 + Hb ⇌ HbCO2). Oxygen is carried two ways: mostly bound to haemoglobin, with a small amount dissolved in plasma.

Reasoning · why CO2 is really the master variable

Look at the carbonic-anhydrase equation. Every extra CO2 molecule that dissolves pushes the reaction right, generating an H+ ion — so blood CO2 and blood pH are two readings of the same thing. That is why "regulate three variables" is almost "regulate CO2": control CO2 and pH largely follows. It also explains why the body can afford to sense O2 less tightly — haemoglobin is nearly fully saturated across a wide PO2 range, so O2 content is buffered, whereas pH is not. (The full acid–base chemistry is the renal unit's job; here we just need the link.)

§1.2Normal ranges — defining "abnormal"

If a value outside the normal range is pathological, then sensors must exist to detect the deviation and feed back to the respiratory (and cardiovascular) systems. Here are the reference ranges the sensors defend:

Normal arterial blood gases, pH & bicarbonate
ParameterLowNormalHigh
paO2< 80 mmHg80–100 mmHg> 100 mmHg
O2 saturation< 95 %95–99 %N/A
paCO2< 35 mmHg35–45 mmHg> 45 mmHg
pH< 7.35 (acidosis)7.35–7.45> 7.45 (alkalosis)
HCO3−< 22 mEq/L22–26 mEq/L> 26 mEq/L
Clinical / real-world · acidosis & alkalosis

A pH below 7.35 is acidosis; above 7.45, alkalosis. Each is sub-classified by origin: respiratory (a CO2 problem — e.g. hypoventilation retaining CO2 → respiratory acidosis) or metabolic (a HCO3− problem). Because CO2 is a gas the lungs control minute-to-minute, ventilation is the body's fastest lever on pH — hold your breath and pH falls within seconds. Reading an arterial blood gas (ABG) — is the pH off? is CO2 or HCO3− to blame? — is a core clinical skill, and the subject of this week's online module.

Memory hook · the numbers that matter

"40 & 40, 7-point-4": arterial CO2 ~40 mmHg, venous ~46, and pH sits at ~7.4. O2 lives in the 80–100 club.

R Recall checklist — blood parameters
  • Three regulated variables — O2, CO2, pH (and pH tracks CO2).
  • Gas moves high → low partial pressure — always.
  • Carbonic anhydrase — CO2+H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H++HCO3−; ↑CO2 ⇒ ↓pH.
  • Carriage — CO2: dissolved/bicarbonate/carbamino; O2: Hb-bound + dissolved.
  • Normals — paO2 80–100, paCO2 35–45, pH 7.35–7.45, HCO3− 22–26.
§2Chemoreceptors · LO3

Chemoreceptors — reading the blood

Two sets of sensors, a clean division of labour: one for O2, both for CO2.

These are the "sensors" from Plate 0.1. There are two populations — peripheral (out in the great vessels) and central (in the brainstem). Their differences aren't arbitrary; each is placed and wired to sense what it can best reach. (Note: chemoreceptors also feed the cardiovascular centres — that's Week 6. Here we follow only their input to breathing.)

§2.1Peripheral chemoreceptors

They sit in the carotid bodies (at the carotid bifurcation) and aortic bodies (off the aortic arch). Each is fed by a tiny artery, and each minute receives roughly twenty times its own weight in arterial blood. That extraordinary flow is the point: they are sampling arterial, not venous, blood — a true read-out of what is being delivered to the body. They respond to three things: oxygen, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen ions.

Label Key — the peripheral sensor array
Carotid body
Chemoreceptor at the carotid bifurcation; its afferents run in the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) — the dominant driver of the ventilatory response to low O2.
Aortic body
Chemoreceptor on the aortic arch; afferents run in the vagus nerve (CN X). Same job, second location.
Glossopharyngeal nerve
Carries the carotid-body signal to the medulla — remember this name; it reappears as the respiratory centre's key input nerve in §4.
Vagus nerve
Carries the aortic-body signal (and many other respiratory reflexes) to the brainstem.
Medulla
Destination of both afferents — where the readings are processed (§4).

The oxygen response — a hockey stick

Plate 2.2 shows why we can afford to sense O2 loosely most of the time. Across the range of normal arterial PO2, ventilation barely responds; at high PO2 there is almost no response at all. Only once PO2 falls below normal does ventilation climb steeply. The peripheral chemoreceptors are the body's main oxygen sensor, and they are built to shout only when oxygen is genuinely low.

Label Key — reading the O2 curve
x-axis (reversed)
Arterial PO2, plotted high → low left to right, so "getting worse" moves rightward.
Red band
The normal arterial PO2 zone (~80–100 mmHg). Across it the curve is nearly flat.
Steep tail (right)
Below normal PO2, ventilation rises sharply — the hypoxic drive kicking in.
Flat left end
Above-normal PO2 buys almost no extra ventilation — more O2 isn't a stimulus.

The carbon-dioxide response — a steep straight line

CO2 is different. Plate 2.3 shows ventilation rising almost linearly and steeply with arterial PCO2 — small rises in CO2 produce large increases in breathing. This is the moment-to-moment throttle on ventilation.

Label Key — reading the CO2 curve
y-axis
Alveolar ventilation in L/min — real output, from a few L/min to >50 L/min.
Threshold (~35 mmHg)
Below this the drive is minimal; above it ventilation climbs almost linearly.
Steep slope
A small PCO2 rise → a large ventilation rise: CO2 is the fine, fast controller of breathing.
Reasoning · O2 and CO2 sensitivities interact (the composite curves)

The two stimuli are not independent. Lower arterial PO2 raises the peripheral chemoreceptors' sensitivity to CO2 (the CO2 response gets steeper), and a lower pH — itself caused by rising CO2 via the bicarbonate reaction — shifts the CO2 response leftward (more ventilation for the same CO2). In other words, hypoxia and acidosis each make the sensor more twitchy to CO2. And crucially, the peripheral chemoreceptors respond to CO2 about 7× more strongly and 5× faster than the central ones — they are the rapid-alarm system, even though (see §2.2) the central receptors set the long-run baseline.

Memory hook · what the periphery is for

Peripheral = "the panic sensors": the only ones that watch O2, and the fast & strong ones for CO2 (7× / 5×).

§2.2Central chemoreceptors

The breathing centres of the brainstem are themselves directly chemosensitive. But their profile looks paradoxical at first:

  • Highly sensitive to H+ — H+ is what they actually detect.
  • Yet blood H+ barely affects them — because H+ ions do not readily cross the blood–brain barrier.
  • Not directly sensitive to CO2, and not particularly sensitive to O2.

So how do they end up modifying ventilation in response to blood gases at all? Through a neat trick of the blood–brain barrier:

blood CO2 → crosses BBB → CSF CO2 → (carbonic anhydrase) → H+ + HCO3− → sensed

CO2 crosses the blood–brain barrier easily (H+ cannot). When blood CO2 rises, cerebrospinal-fluid CO2 rises with it; in the CSF it is converted to H+ and HCO3−; and the central chemoreceptors — exquisitely tuned to H+ — sense that CSF H+. The net effect: central chemoreceptors are highly sensitive to blood CO2, but not to blood H+.

Reasoning · the blood–brain-barrier paradox resolved

It sounds contradictory that a receptor "senses CO2 but not H+" while its actual stimulus is H+. The barrier is the key. The BBB is lipid — it waves through the small, uncharged, lipid-soluble CO2 molecule but blocks the charged H+ ion. So circulating H+ is fenced out (blood acidosis doesn't directly reach them), while CO2 slips in and is converted to H+ on the brain side, where it is detected. The receptor's true stimulus is CSF H+; its effective blood stimulus is CO2.

Memory hook · who senses what

Central Chases CO2 (via CSF H+). Peripheral is the only one that watches O2. Both feel CO2 — periphery faster, centre steadier.

Clinical / real-world · the hypoxic drive in chronic CO2 retainers

Normally CO2 (via the central receptors) is the main driver of breathing. But in people who retain CO2 chronically (e.g. severe COPD), the CSF slowly buffers with HCO3−, so the central CO2 drive dulls — and breathing comes to lean more on the peripheral hypoxic drive (Plate 2.2's steep low-O2 tail). It's why giving uncontrolled high-flow oxygen to a minority of such patients can blunt their remaining stimulus to breathe. It also explains why the carotid body, tiny as it is, is clinically indispensable.

R Recall checklist — chemoreceptors
  • Peripheral — carotid + aortic bodies; sample arterial blood (~20× their weight/min); sense O2, CO2, H+.
  • O2 response — flat until PO2 drops below normal, then steep (hypoxic drive).
  • CO2 response — steep & linear; periphery is 7× stronger & 5× faster than centre.
  • Interactions — low PO2 and low pH both raise CO2 sensitivity.
  • Central — sense CSF H+; CO2 crosses the BBB (H+ can't) → sensitive to blood CO2, not blood H+ or O2.
§3Reflexes · LO4

Reflexes & receptors

Beyond the blood gases: the involuntary inputs that stop, protect, or ramp up breathing.

A reflex is the sum total of a particular involuntary activity. Chemoreceptors track the blood; this section covers the other sensors that reach the respiratory centre — some to halt breathing, some to protect the airway, and several to drive it up.

§3.1Stopping breathing: Hering–Breuer & apnoea

The Hering–Breuer reflex uses stretch receptors in the bronchi and bronchioles. At high levels of stretch they signal via the vagi to cease inspiration — but only during hyperinflation (tidal volume greater than about 3× normal). It is a safety cut-out, not a normal part of quiet breathing.

Apnoea is the cessation of breathing for a period. It can be:

  • Centrally caused — loss of the pacing signal from the respiratory centre.
  • Physically caused — e.g. relaxation of the soft palate occluding the airway.
  • Reflex — via the juxtacapillary ("J") receptors in the alveolar wall, in contact with the capillaries. They produce apnoea and are stimulated by pulmonary congestion, pneumonia, and chemicals such as histamine and serotonin.

After apnoea breaks, there is usually a reflex burst of increased rate/depth — because during the pause blood O2 fell and CO2 rose, stimulating the chemoreceptors of §2. The loop always reasserts itself.

Reasoning · why Hering–Breuer only fires at hyperinflation

If stretch receptors ended every normal breath, they would fight the respiratory centre's own rhythm and cap tidal volume far too low. Setting their threshold high (>~3× normal) makes them a protective backstop against over-inflation (barotrauma) that stays silent during ordinary breathing — present when you need it, invisible when you don't. Good control systems reserve their emergency brakes for emergencies.

§3.2Driving breathing up: five receptor types

At least four (here, five) receptor types can raise minute ventilation, sometimes to the point of hyperventilation:

  • Irritant receptors — in the lungs, stimulated by harmful chemicals (ammonia, sulphur dioxide). They trigger reflex hyperventilation and bronchospasm, narrowing airways to keep the chemical out of the alveoli.
  • Proprioceptors — position sensors in joints, muscles and tendons. Activated immediately by dynamic exercise, raising rate/depth even before oxygen demand has actually risen.
  • Metaboreceptors — peripheral nerve endings (mainly in skeletal muscle) responding to local metabolites: CO2, H+, lactate.
  • Thermoreceptors — mostly cutaneous; both high and low body temperature can raise ventilation.
  • Pain receptors — pain signals to the respiratory centre and can drive a hyperventilatory response.
Reasoning · why metaboreceptors ≠ chemoreceptors, and why proprioceptors fire first

Two easy confusions, both worth nailing. Metaboreceptors vs chemoreceptors: chemoreceptors (carotid/aortic bodies, brainstem) sense circulating arterial gases and H+; metaboreceptors sense the local chemical environment inside a working muscle. Different place, different sample. Proprioceptor feed-forward: if breathing only rose after exercise had already dropped blood O2, you'd spend every sprint playing catch-up. Instead, movement itself pre-emptively drives ventilation — anticipating the demand rather than reacting to a deficit. Feedback corrects; feed-forward prevents.

Memory hook · the five that push ventilation up

Irritant · Proprioceptor · Metaboreceptor · Thermoreceptor · Pain — "I Pump More, The Pace."

Clinical / real-world · when these inputs dominate

J receptors are why left-heart failure and pulmonary oedema cause rapid, shallow, distressing breathing (and, in the extreme, apnoea): congested capillaries stimulate the alveolar-wall receptors directly. Irritant receptors underlie the bronchospasm of an asthma or chemical exposure. And note the caveat from the slides: not every rise in rate is "hyperventilation" — true hyperventilation means blowing off too much CO2 (hypocapnia), which is why over-breathing causes tingling and light-headedness.

§3.3Protective reflexes: cough, sneeze, swallow

  • Cough — protective reflex from irritation of the airway below the nose (larynx, trachea, bronchi), carried by the vagus. A deep inspiration is followed by forceful expiration against a closed glottis; intrapleural pressure rises above 100 mmHg; the glottis then snaps open and air blasts out at up to 160 km/h, expelling the irritant.
  • Sneeze — the same machinery, but triggered by irritation of the nasal mucous membrane.
  • Deglutition (swallowing) — during a swallow, respiration is briefly arrested: a "swallowing apnoea." It stops food entering the airway; you can see the hyoid elevate and the epiglottis close during the swallow.

§3.4Summary — every reflex input, and where it converges

Respiratory receptors — location, stimulus & reflex
ReceptorLocatedSensesReflex / effect
Central chemoreceptorsBrainstem (medulla)Blood CO2 (via CSF H+)Alter minute ventilation
Peripheral chemoreceptorsCarotid / aortic bodiesBlood O2, CO2, H+Alter minute ventilation
Juxtacapillary (J)Alveolar wallCongestion, chemicalsApnoea
IrritantRespiratory epitheliumAirborne irritantsCough, sneeze, bronchospasm
StretchBronchi / bronchiolesHyperinflationHering–Breuer (cease inspiration)
ProprioceptorsJoints, muscles, tendonsMovement↑ minute ventilation
MetaboreceptorsSkeletal muscleLocal metabolites↑ minute ventilation
ThermoreceptorsUnder the skinTemperatureAlter minute ventilation

Every one of these arrows lands in the same box. Plate 3.1 is the convergence map — chemoreceptors, higher brain, and all the reflex receptors feeding a single respiratory centre, whose only output is to the respiratory muscles.

Label Key — the convergence
Inputs (left)
Every sensor from §2–§3 plus higher-brain routes — emotional stimuli and the motor cortex (voluntary/anticipatory control).
Respiratory centre (middle)
The single processing hub; it sums all inputs and issues one decision.
Output (right)
One efferent path to the respiratory muscles, which alter breathing rate and tidal volume — nothing else.
R Recall checklist — reflexes & receptors
  • Hering–Breuer — bronchial stretch receptors → vagus → cease inspiration; only at hyperinflation (>3× TV).
  • Apnoea — central (no pacing), physical (soft-palate), or reflex (J receptors).
  • J receptors — alveolar wall; congestion/pneumonia/histamine/serotonin → apnoea.
  • Five up-drivers — Irritant, Proprioceptor, Metaboreceptor, Thermoreceptor, Pain ("I Pump More, The Pace").
  • Protective — cough (airway, vagal, glottis >100 mmHg, 160 km/h), sneeze (nasal), deglutition apnoea.
  • Hyperventilation = excess CO2 loss (hypocapnia), not just fast breathing.
§4Respiratory centre · LO5

The respiratory centre

The processing hub — its brainstem anatomy, its rhythm, and the nerves it commands.

This is the "processing centre" from Plate 0.1. Whatever the input — a low PO2, a proprioceptor, a fright — the centre can do only one thing: change minute ventilation = respiratory rate × tidal volume. Central control is genuinely complex and still being mapped, but its essential parts and wiring are clear.

Label Key — the centre's components
DRG — dorsal respiratory group
In the medulla; generates the basic pacemaker and the inspiratory "ramp" (the smoothly rising drive that sets tidal volume), and is the input site for glossopharyngeal (peripheral chemoreceptor) signals.
VRG — ventral respiratory group
In the medulla; inactive during quiet breathing, recruited for forced inspiration and expiration when demand rises. Outputs to expiratory, pharynx, larynx and tongue muscles.
Pre-Bötzinger complex
Part of the medullary rhythm machinery driving the pacemaker.
NTS (nucleus tractus solitarius)
The medullary relay receiving visceral/sensory afferents.
PRG — pontine respiratory group
In the pons; fine-tunes the medullary rhythm and links to higher brain centres. Contains the pneumotaxic & apneustic influences below.
Medullary chemoreceptors
The central chemoreceptors of §2.2, monitoring CO2 (as CSF H+) right at the centre.
Outputs
Two efferent streams: primarily to the diaphragm, and to the expiratory/airway muscles.
Simplified central pathways — who does what
GroupRole
Pneumotaxic centre (pons)Arrests the duration of the inspiratory phase and increases respiratory rate — it caps each breath and quickens the tempo.
Apneustic centre (pons)Increases the depth of inspiration — deepens each breath.
Dorsal respiratory group (DRG)Generates the pacemaker signal and the respiratory ramp (volume inspired); input site for glossopharyngeal chemoreceptor signals.
Ventral respiratory group (VRG)Inactive in normal breathing; contributes to inspiration and expiration when ventilatory demand is high.
Reasoning · how transection experiments locate the rhythm

Where is breathing actually generated? Cut the brainstem at different levels and watch. Sever the pons (leaving the medulla): breathing continues, but its smooth sinus-like rhythm is lost — so the pons shapes the rhythm but doesn't create it. Sever the medulla: breathing stops entirely. The conclusion is clean — the medulla holds the obligatory rhythm generator (DRG / pre-Bötzinger), while the pons (PRG, with its pneumotaxic and apneustic influences) fine-tunes rate and depth. Subtract a part, see what breaks, infer its job.

Memory hook · dorsal vs ventral, pons on top

DRG = Default driver (quiet breathing & the ramp). VRG = Vigorous reserve (forced breathing only). Pneumotaxic taps the brakes on inspiration; Apneustic Amplifies depth.

§4.1Inputs and outputs of the centre

Inputs to the respiratory centre: higher-order brain centres (responding to environmental stressors), the peripheral chemoreceptors (arriving via the glossopharyngeal nerve), the central chemoreceptors (right there in the intracranial space), and the other sensory nerves of §3. Outputs go via somatic motor neurons to the breathing muscles. Plate 4.2 shows the actual nerves.

Label Key — the wiring in the body
Respiratory centre (medulla oblongata)
The processing hub, sitting in the brainstem.
Glossopharyngeal nerve + carotid body
The main input (afferent) line: peripheral chemoreceptor readings arriving at the centre.
Phrenic nerve → diaphragm
Output (efferent) to the diaphragm — the principal muscle of inspiration. (From spinal roots C3–C5.)
Intercostal nerves → intercostal muscles
Output to the intercostal muscles of the chest wall, adjusting the ribcage.
Spinal cord
The cable relaying the centre's commands down to the phrenic and intercostal motor neurons.
Clinical / real-world · "severing the medulla" pharmacologically

You don't need a scalpel to silence the medullary centre. Opioids depress it directly — an overdose causes the respiratory rate to fall and then stop (the reversal drug, naloxone, works here). General anaesthetics and deep sedation blunt the same centre, which is why anaesthetised patients are ventilated. Rare disorders make the point too: in congenital central hypoventilation ("Ondine's curse") the automatic drive fails, and a brainstem stroke at the wrong spot can abolish breathing — the living version of the transection experiment.

R Recall checklist — the respiratory centre
  • Only output — minute ventilation = rate × tidal volume.
  • DRG — pacemaker + inspiratory ramp; glossopharyngeal input site. VRG — quiet-rest silent, drives forced breathing.
  • Pons — pneumotaxic (limits inspiration, ↑rate) & apneustic (↑depth) fine-tuning.
  • Transection — cut pons: rhythm ragged but breathing continues; cut medulla: no breathing (medulla = generator).
  • In — glossopharyngeal (peripheral chemo), central chemo, higher brain, sensory reflexes. Out — phrenic (diaphragm), intercostal (intercostals).
§5Synthesis · exam

Putting it together

One chain that answers every "why did breathing change?" question.

This is how to communicate respiratory regulation — as a professional, and in Assessment 2 or the final exam. Any change in breathing can, and should, be written as a single chain:

change → detected how? → processed how? → output where? → action

It is just Plate 0.1's loop, straightened into a sentence. Fill each arrow with a named structure and you have both the mechanism and a full-marks answer. The action always resolves to a change in rate and/or tidal volume — i.e. minute ventilation.

Worked example · one mechanism that raises O2 intake during walking

Question (paraphrasing the lecture): name one mechanism that increases oxygen intake during walking, and trace it through the chain.

  1. Change: walking is movement — the stimulus. (Note: this happens before blood O2 has actually fallen.)
  2. Detected how: movement stimulates proprioceptors in joints, muscles and tendons (§3.2).
  3. Processed how: proprioceptor afferents signal the respiratory centre of the medulla (§4).
  4. Output where: increased activity in the phrenic and intercostal nerves (Plate 4.2).
  5. Action: increased breathing rate and tidal volume → higher minute ventilation = rate × tidal volume → raised alveolar PO2 → greater O2 diffusion into blood (§1).

Answer: movement → proprioceptors → respiratory centre → phrenic/intercostal nerves → ↑ rate & tidal volume → ↑ minute ventilation and O2 uptake — a feed-forward response that anticipates demand rather than waiting for a deficit.

Reasoning · why the chain is the whole unit in one line

Every section maps onto one arrow. §1 defines the variable that changes; §2–§3 supply the detectors; §4 is the processing and output; and the action is always minute ventilation. If you can name a structure for each link, you have understood the lecture — and if you can't fill an arrow, that's exactly the gap to revise. (The vasomotor cortex also engages during exercise to match perfusion to ventilation — but that's later in the unit.)

R Recall checklist — synthesis
  • The chain — change → detected how → processed how → output where → action.
  • The action — always a change in rate and/or tidal volume (minute ventilation).
  • Walking example — movement → proprioceptors → respiratory centre → phrenic/intercostal → ↑ ventilation (feed-forward).
  • Exam habit — never say breathing changed because someone "thought" it should; name the detected change.
